text:
The newly agreed expansion of the Korea-China free trade agreement is expected to give a significant boost to Korea's travel industry by opening direct sales channels in China and encouraging broader bilateral tourism exchanges, industry experts said Thursday.
While major Korean package tour operators may not immediately jump into competing directly with Chinese travel agencies, the deal will help add more flights between the two countries and boost both inbound and outbound travel demand, they added.
On Wednesday, Korea and China reached a substantial conclusion in their follow-up free trade agreement negotiations on services and investment during a bilateral summit held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said.
Under the upgraded pact, Korean travel agencies established in 23 designated regions across China will be permitted to directly recruit Chinese group tourists and sell overseas tour packages to both Chinese citizens and foreign residents.
The designated areas cover 11 pilot zones, including Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Hainan, along with 12 pilot free trade zones in provinces such as Guangdong, Henan, Hubei and Sichuan. According to the Korea Association of Travel Agents (KATA), the 11 pilot zones alone had a combined resident population of 188.82 million as of the end of 2025.
Industry groups welcomed the breakthrough as a long-awaited opportunity to expand their footprint.
"This will serve as a historic milestone that expands entry into the Chinese market, a long-cherished wish of our travel industry, and elevates bilateral tourism exchanges to the next level," KATA Chairman Lee Jin-seok said.
Major domestic package tour agencies, which mainly focus on outbound travel for Koreans, see the agreement as a broader catalyst for market recovery, rather than an immediate entry into China's local inbound sector.
"Since major domestic package travel agencies barely operate inbound businesses, there may be no immediate direct impact from running local operations in China, especially given the risks of competing against established local players," an official from Yellow Balloon, a travel agency in Seoul, said.
"However, we are focusing on the broader trend of improving bilateral relations and more active exchanges," the official added.
The government expects the deal to help Korean agencies earn new revenue by offering tours themed around K-pop, Korean skin care and food, as well as regional travel programs across Korea. Agencies will also have room to expand their business scope by linking Korean itineraries with third-country destinations such as Japan and Southeast Asia.
The opening comes as Chinese visitors to Korea continue to rebound. According to the Korea Tourism Data Lab, 5.47 million Chinese tourists visited Korea from January through September this year, up 29.2 percent from the same period a year earlier. That nine-month figure nearly matches last year's full-year total of 5.48 million.
Chinese travelers made up 32 percent of all foreign visitors during the first nine months of this year, continuing a steady rise from 29.7 percent in 2024 and 30.1 percent in 2025. They also tend to spend more than other tourists, averaging $1,504 per person last year, which was 13 percent higher than the overall foreign visitor average.
"If this momentum continues, airlines will expand flight routes between the two countries, which will create a favorable environment that boosts not only inbound traffic but also Korean outbound demand to China next year, allowing us to develop more diverse products beyond traditional destinations like Zhangjiajie and Mount Baekdu,” the travel agency official added.
